routes.label: Multiply complex coordinates and subtract clipped corner triangles

question:
A region \(S\) in the complex plane is defined by \[ \scriptsize S = \{x + iy : -1 \le x \le 1,\ -1 \le y \le 1\}. \]

A complex number \(z = x + iy\) is chosen uniformly at random from \(S.\) What is the probability that \(\left(\dfrac{3}{4} + \dfrac{3}{4}i\right)z\) is also in \(S?\)
solution:
Because the point is chosen uniformly from the square, the probability is the favorable area divided by the square's area. Expanding the complex product tells us which points are favorable:
\[
\left(\frac34+\frac34i\right)(x+iy)
=\frac34(x-y)+\frac34(x+y)i.
\]
Thus the product belongs to \(S\) exactly when
\[
-\frac43\le x-y\le\frac43,
\qquad
-\frac43\le x+y\le\frac43.
\]
Inside the original square, these inequalities cut off its four corners. For example, the forbidden region \(x+y>4/3\) lies near \((1,1)\). Its boundary meets the top and right sides at \((1/3,1)\) and \((1,1/3)\), so it is a right triangle with both legs of length \(2/3\). Its area is
\[
\frac12\left(\frac23\right)^2=\frac29.
\]
The other three violations give congruent triangles at the other corners. Each lies in a different quadrant, so they do not overlap, and every excluded point violates one of the four bounds above. The boundary lines have area zero, so including their points does not change the probability.

The original square has area \(2\cdot2=4\). Therefore the desired probability is
\[
\frac{4-4(2/9)}{4}=\frac79.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{\frac79}\), choice D.
